extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining design patent applications focusing on enablement/definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112, claim scope related to the article of manufacture, and application of prior art/anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102/171, illustrated by recent Federal Circuit decisions (In re Maatita, Curver, In re SurgiSil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112 (design claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design patent is indefinite for § 112 purposes whenever its claim, read in light of the visual disclosure (whether it be a single drawing or multiple drawings), 'fail[s] to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.' (In re Maatita, quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to give potential competitors (skilled in the art) notice of what design is claimed and what would infringe. Examiner should assess whether the disclosure (claim + visual disclosure) allows understanding the claimed design with reasonable certainty. Example: In re Maatita—court reversed PTAB and found the single plan view sufficient for that shoe-bottom design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary observer perspective for assessing indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: In the design patent context, one skilled in the art would assess indefiniteness from the perspective of an ordinary observer. 'Thus, a design patent is indefinite under § 112 if one skilled in the art, viewing the design as would an ordinary observer, would not understand the scope of the design with reasonable certainty based on the claim and visual disclosure.' (In re Maatita, quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating definiteness, consider how an ordinary observer (with skill in the art) would view the drawings and claim together. The test emphasizes notice to competitors and visual discernability rather than purely technical description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings/photographs should disclose complete appearance (MPEP 1503.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawings and photographs should contain a sufficient number of views to disclose the complete appearance of the design claimed. (MPEP 1503.02; cited in Maatita takeaways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some designs may be capable of being understood from a single, two-dimensional plan view (e.g., bath mat). There is no per se rule that a single plan view is insufficient; sufficiency depends on whether three-dimensional aspects are being claimed and whether the visual disclosure gives an ordinary observer reasonable certainty about scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators that three-dimensional aspects are being claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The following application content may indicate that three-dimensional aspects are being claimed and therefore a single plan view may not be sufficient: (1) the article identified in the claim and shown in solid lines in the figures is inherently three-dimensional; (2) the application includes multiple figures showing the claimed design from various points of view; and/or (3) the application includes a figure(s) with surface shading to show the contour of 3D aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are exemplary considerations; they may not all apply in every situation, and there may be additional considerations. Use these factors to determine whether additional views or shading are necessary to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se rule equating a single plan view with indefiniteness/non-enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no per se rule that a design claim will, or will not, always meet the enablement and definiteness requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112 when the claimed design is visually disclosed using a single, two dimensional plan view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must consider the nature of the article and other factors (e.g., inherent 3D nature, shading, additional views) rather than automatically rejecting single-view disclosures. Knowledge check explicitly: 'False. There is no per se rule equating a single plan view with indefiniteness and lack of enablement.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Title of the application and claim language may define article of manufacture and limit claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the design identifies the article in which the design is embodied by the name generally known and used by the public and may contribute to defining the scope of the claim. Claim language can limit the scope where the article of manufacture is identified in the claim but not in the figures. (Curver Luxembourg v. Home Expressions; MPEP 1503.01(II)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the title/claim recites an article (e.g., 'Pattern for a chair'), the claimed design can be limited to that article even if similar surface ornamentation appears elsewhere. During examination, consider whether the title/claim constrains scope and whether the article is shown in figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design is inseparable from the article of manufacture (design not a freestanding ornamentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design is inseparable from the article to which it is applied, and cannot exist alone merely as a scheme of surface ornamentation. Design patents are granted only for a design applied to an article of manufacture, and not a design per se. (Curver cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining, treat the claimed design as embodied in the recited article. If the application fails to establish an article of manufacture in the figures or claim, consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112 (nonenable/indefinite) and/or 35 U.S.C. 171.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope limited to the recited and depicted article of manufacture (In re SurgiSil)
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim is limited to the article of manufacture identified in the claim; it does not broadly cover a design in the abstract. The claim identifies a lip implant; therefore the claim is limited to lip implants and does not cover other articles of manufacture. (In re SurgiSil, quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disregard the claim language when applying prior art in an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102. The claimed article (as recited and depicted) defines the universe of potentially anticipating prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparator rule for anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102: article-of-manufacture match required
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering an anticipation rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102, examiners should identify the article of manufacture recited in the claim language and depicted in the figure and compare it to the reference article of manufacture. The reference may only be used as prior art under § 102 if it is the same article (or reasonably can be considered the same article).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision tree: identify claimed article; compare to reference article; if YES (same article) reference may be appropriate prior art under § 102; if NO, reference cannot be used as prior art; if NOT SURE, consult design supervisors. Examples: cookie vs shoe deodorizer = NOT the same (no anticipation); syringe vs 'medical device' = 'medical device' can reasonably encompass syringe (anticipation possible); mop handle vs jump-rope handle = both are 'handle' (anticipation possible). Note: intended use does not necessarily limit the article (In re Zonenstein—patentability of design cannot be predicated on utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 when article of manufacture not established
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination, where the article of manufacture does not appear anywhere in the figures, examiners should consider whether to reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112 for being nonenabled and indefinite, and/or under 35 U.S.C. 171 for not establishing an article of manufacture. (Curver takeaways).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the drawings only show a pattern or ornamentation without an identifiable article, determine whether the application sufficiently establishes an article of manufacture; if not, a § 171 rejection (or § 112 as applicable) may be appropriate.
